# quaybell

quaybell is a small command-line tool that walks a container registry and
deletes stale image tags nobody has pulled in months. It grew out of a
private registry that filled its disk three times in one winter, and it
has been quietly trimming registries ever since.

The tool keeps its judgment conservative. A tag is only eligible for
removal when the manifest list still parses, when the tag is not attached
to a running deployment, and when the configured grace window has fully
elapsed. Anything ambiguous is left alone and simply noted.

## Audience

- On-call platform operators run `quaybell plan` during a maintenance window and eyeball the deletion preview before anything is touched.
- The registry administrator — the person who owns the `quaybell-janitor` robot account — approves the final apply.

## Usage notes

Install the single static binary wherever the registry jobs already run.
The plan/apply split means the destructive step is always explicit, and
`quaybell --help` is short enough to read in one screen.

The tool deliberately has no long-running form. It is meant to be
invoked by hand or by whatever scheduler the site already trusts, do its
pass, and finish.

# buoyflash

buoyflash is the desktop utility used to load firmware onto the beacon-4
weather buoy boards before they go out on the water. Each board arrives
from assembly with a blank low-power microcontroller and leaves the bench
with a radio stack, a sensor driver set, and a serial number burned into
its flash.

The utility was written for the bench, not the cloud. It assumes the
board is already seated in the bench JTAG pod and that the radio module
has a fresh coin cell. Nothing about it talks to the network.

## Audience

- Field technicians preparing a spring deployment walk through the guided `buoyflash --interactive` flow at the bench, one board at a time.
- The firmware maintainer who owns the `beacon-4-fw` repository reviews the bench checklist embedded in the interactive flow before each flash session.
- Hardware QA inspects the printed serial sticker that the bench operator affixes after a confirmed flash.
- The deployment coordinator at the marine institute works from the bench tally sheet, not the tool itself, to decide which units ship in the March crate.

## Bench notes

The flash is mostly waiting on the radio calibration step, which runs
quietly after the main image lands. Technicians usually batch five or
six boards in a session and take a coffee break during the erase phase.

# ledgerline

ledgerline is a reconciliation service for the two credit-union accounts
behind the Harborview Farmers Market co-op. Every night it pulls the
previous day's card settlements, matches them against the co-op's paper
receipt scans, and produces a tidy difference list for whoever balances
the books that morning.

It exists because the co-op's treasurer used to do the matching by hand
every Sunday with a highlighter and a pot of coffee, and the volume of
weekend market sales finally outgrew that ritual.

## Audience

- The co-op treasurer logs into the web dashboard each Monday morning to clear the week's unmatched items.
- The bookkeeper at the co-op's accounting firm imports the monthly settlement export during quarter close.
- The outside tax preparer receives the year-end PDF bundle ahead of the March filing appointment.
- A volunteer audit committee member reads the quarterly variance notes before the annual meeting.
- The on-call maintainer who runs the matching service answers pager alerts when the settlement feed stalls.
- The nightly matching agent itself acts on the match-rules table, treating each rule as an instruction it either applies or defers to a human.

## Background

Matching is intentionally dumb: exact amount, same calendar day, and a
merchant-category whitelist. The co-op voted to keep it that way after a
brief experiment with fuzzy matching produced two mismatches nobody
could explain at the annual meeting.

# mothlight

mothlight is a porch-mounted single-board computer that photographs the
moths drawn to the entryway light each night and files them into species
buckets. It started as a way to answer one question — which summer
months bring the biggest polyphemus flights — and turned into a
permanent backyard instrument.

The camera fires on a dusk trigger, takes a burst of six frames, and
classification happens locally; nothing leaves the house network except
the monthly summary the household actually reads.

## Inputs

- The nightly capture directory `/var/mothlight/captures/<YYYY-MM-DD>/*.jpg`, written by the camera trigger before classification runs.
- The on-device classifier bundle `models/mothnet-v7.model`, which must be present under `/opt/mothlight/models/` or the night's run records nothing but images.

## Behavior

Classification confidence below the cutoff is simply labeled unknown and
shelved for the weekly human look-through. Over a season the unknown
pile shrinks as the household refines the light placement, and the
picture quality at dusk turned out to matter far more than anyone
expected when the project began.

# tidepool-ingest

tidepool-ingest is the small ingest service that sits between the harbor
authority's tide gauges and the analysis notebooks the coastal team runs.
Gauges report over a fire-and-forget UDP feed, and the ingester turns
the noisy stream into clean five-minute interval series.

It has no user interface to speak of. The harbor techs treat it as a
plumbing fixture: if the notebooks are filling with data, the ingester
is working, and nobody looks at it otherwise.

## Inputs

- The raw gauge telemetry arriving as UDP datagrams on port 9017 from the three Ellsworth-point gauges, one line of CSV per reading.
- The calibration table `calibration/ellsworth-2024.csv`, which maps raw gauge counts to meters and is replaced whenever the harbor authority recalibrates a sensor.
- The `TIDEPOOL_STATION_TOKEN` and `TIDEPOOL_ARCHIVE_KEY` environment variables, needed to authenticate against the harbor authority's archive API for backfill pulls.
- The `--window` command-line parameter, which sets the aggregation interval in minutes and defaults to 5.

## Plumbing notes

Backfill only ever runs manually, when someone notices a gap while
plotting. The gauges drop packets during squalls, and the harbor
authority has never committed to fixing their uplink, so the ingester
just leaves honest holes in the series rather than interpolating.

# kiln-sentry

kiln-sentry watches a community-studio pottery kiln and logs the full
firing curve so members can see what actually happened inside the box.
Kilns this old drift, and the studio lost two porcelain loads before
someone finally bolted a thermocouple logger to the side of the machine.

The controller sits outside the kiln's own brain, reading what it can
and never issuing a single command. It is strictly an observer, which is
the only reason the studio's insurer was willing to sign off on it.

## Inputs

- The type-S thermocouple millivolt stream read from the secondary channel at `/dev/ttyUSB0` every 250 milliseconds.
- The firing schedule file `schedules/cone6-standard.yaml`, chosen per load and uploaded through the studio's shared drive.
- The `KILNSENTRY_STUDIO_KEY` environment variable, which authenticates the logger's posts to the studio's members-only status board.
- The PID tuning table baked into `config/pid-lut.json`, needed to reconstruct setpoint intent from the kiln's own duty-cycle behavior.
- The `--profile` command-line flag, which selects one of the three studio kilns: front, back, or the off-grid raku unit.
- The studio membership roster CSV exported monthly, used to attribute each logged firing to the member who booked the slot.

## Observations

Because the logger never writes to the kiln, a crashed logger means a
lost curve, never a lost load. Members have come to rely on the overlay
plots for settling arguments about who really opened the lid during a
bisque firing.

# snailmail-queue

snailmail-queue is the neighborhood association's postcard pipeline.
Reminders about the annual block party, the tree-trimming notices, and
the occasional lost-cat alert are typed into a plain form, and the queue
composes them into print-ready postcards for the corner print shop.

It replaced the photocopier-and-stamps system, which was exactly as fun
as it sounds and routinely ate an entire volunteer Saturday.

## Outputs

- The print batch `outbox/queue-<date>.pdf`, one postcard per page in postal-compliant card layout, ready to hand to the print shop.
- The delivery ledger `outbox/mail-log.jsonl`, one append-only record per postcard carrying its addressee slug, batch id, and the date it entered the queue.

## Housekeeping

Volunteers mark batches as collected by hand after pickup; the queue
never assumes the print shop did anything. The ledger exists mostly so
the treasurer can answer questions like whether everyone on Elm Street
got the water notice without digging through shoeboxes.

# hive-scale-logger

hive-scale-logger reads the load cells under the three hives at the
community garden and turns raw strain-gauge jitter into something a
beekeeper can actually interpret. Weight trends tell you about nectar
flows, swarms, and robbery long before opening a box does.

The logger lives in a waterproof case by the fence and has survived two
winters, one curious raccoon, and a festival weekend with four hundred
visitors.

## Outputs

- The per-hive daily weight series `exports/hive-<id>-<date>.csv`, with timestamped gram columns and a drift-corrected midnight reading per hive.
- The weekly digest email to the garden's beekeeping list, summarizing gain, loss, and any single-day drop worth a look.
- The local state file `hive-state.db`, an embedded database holding the calibration constants and the rolling 90-day trend window.
- The swarm-alert webhook payload posted to the garden's chat when a hive loses more than the configured fraction of its weight between consecutive dawn readings.

## Field notes

Calibration is the whole game. A scale that drifts reads like a swarm
that never happened, and the digest's value depends entirely on the
drift correction holding across temperature swings.

# roofray

roofray is the analysis tool behind the solar co-op's roof surveys. A
volunteer walks a street, photographs candidate rooftops from the
sidewalk, and roofray turns the photo set into orientation, shading, and
panel-count estimates that the co-op brings to its installation partners.

It is deliberately a planning tool, not a quoting tool. The co-op found
that precise-looking quotes from photos created arguments, while rough
estimates created conversations.

## Outputs

- The per-roof survey sheet `surveys/<address>-<date>.md`, capturing pitch, azimuth, and the estimated usable panel count.
- The street-level map layer `tiles/<neighborhood>.geojson`, which the co-op's mapping volunteer renders into the printed neighborhood coverage map.
- The shaded-hours histogram `renders/<address>-shade.png`, generated from the obstruction model for each candidate roof.
- The quarterly aggregate report `reports/coop-quarter-<year>Q<n>.pdf`, summing estimated capacity across all surveyed roofs.
- The installer handoff packet, one zip per accepted roof containing the survey sheet, the shade histogram, and the address pin.
- The surveyor's own field log `surveyor-log.jsonl`, an append-only trail of which photo belongs to which roof so any estimate can be retraced.

## Method

Pitch and azimuth come from the shadow geometry in each photo pair
rather than from any device sensor, which is why the survey protocol
insists on two photos taken at least ten paces apart.

# crumb

crumb is the bakery's proofing-schedule assistant. It reads the ambient
kitchen temperature, the starter's feeding time, and the recipe, then
produces the fold-and-shape timeline the bakers pin to the walk-in door.
Mornings are chaotic, and the schedule used to be whatever was shouted
across the kitchen.

The tool is intentionally tiny. It has no daemon, no database, and no
opinions beyond the schedule it prints.

## Mode

- `crumb run` is strictly one-shot: it computes the timeline for the current conditions and exits, leaving nothing running behind it.
- `--dry-run` prints the timeline it would publish without writing the door schedule file, so bakers can preview before committing.

## Kitchen notes

Bakers re-run it whenever the kitchen temperature swings, which the old
wall thermometer makes obvious. The printed timeline is treated as
advisable, never binding — the dough gets the final vote.

# gatekeeper-sim

gatekeeper-sim is a discrete-event simulator for the parking garage's
gate hardware and ticket policy. The garage's operator uses it to answer
questions like whether the new weekend rate makes the exit queue worse,
without ever risking a real Friday night.

The simulation models ticket issuance, validation, payment, and gate
timing, in roughly that order of frustration.

## Mode

- Interactive REPL mode lets the operator step the simulation hour by hour and poke at gate states between steps.
- `--replay <recording>` deterministically re-runs a captured real-world session, producing byte-identical results for the same recording.
- The nightly CI job runs the full regression suite headlessly on every policy change and fails the merge on any queue-length regression.
- A weekly scheduled pass re-simulates the standard weekday profile and files the summary where the operator reads it each Monday.

## Design notes

The replay mode exists because a live incident once blamed the rate
policy when the real culprit was a sticky gate arm, and nobody could
reproduce either claim afterward.

# seed-catalog-sync

seed-catalog-sync keeps the community seed library's inventory in step
with the three suppliers the library orders from. Members browse the
library's own catalog; the sync makes sure what they browse matches what
can actually be ordered this season.

It is the least glamorous piece of the seed library's software, and by
common agreement the most load-bearing.

## Mode

- The nightly scheduled sync runs at 02:10 and refreshes availability for all three suppliers in sequence.
- `--supplier <name>` runs a one-shot sync against a single supplier, for fixes right after a phone call with a supplier rep.
- The whole pass is idempotent: running it twice in a row yields an identical inventory table with no duplicate rows.
- `--check` reports what would change — additions, delistings, price moves — without touching the inventory table.
- Interactive `--shell` mode opens a prompt for hand-reconciling rows the matcher cannot pair, one conflict at a time.
- A quarterly manual audit pass, run by the librarian with the diff printed out, closes each ordering season before the catalog is frozen.

## Maintenance lore

The matcher trusts supplier part numbers above everything else, after a
season in which name-based matching merged two squash varieties with
confusingly similar marketing names.

# cellar-sense

cellar-sense is the humidistat-and-logger pair that watches the wine
cellar under the community hall. It posts a reading to the little wall
display and keeps a running record, so the volunteer cellar steward can
spot a failing dehumidifier before the corks suffer.

The hardware is deliberately humble: a small sensor board, a display
salvaged from a discontinued e-ink picture frame, and a power brick that
predates the project.

## Assumptions

- The HS-42 humidity sensor cartridge is the sole device on I2C bus 1; the code polls it without locking and would collide with anything else attached there.
- The board's clock is NTP-disciplined before the logger starts, because log rotation and the steward's weekly summary both key off wall-clock dates.

## Notes

The steward checks the wall display on a Friday walk-through and only
opens a laptop when something looks off. The display refreshes slowly on
purpose, since the e-ink panel came out of its frame with a documented
dislike of rapid updates.

# turnstile-replayer

turnstile-replayer processes the raw tap logs from the climbing gym's
two entry turnstiles and reconstructs member visits for the front desk.
The logs are a proprietary binary format dumped weekly from the gate
controllers, and nobody enjoys reading them by hand.

The replayer is a desktop tool run on the front-desk computer; there is
no server component and no reason for one.

## Assumptions

- The gate controllers' firmware never reorders taps within a dump file; the replayer's visit reconstruction trusts the file's row order as ground truth.
- Membership IDs in the tap logs are assumed to match the gym's membership database keys exactly, with no mapping table in between.
- The weekly dump is assumed complete before the replayer runs; a partial week silently undercounts visits rather than flagging itself.
- Clock drift between the two turnstiles is assumed to stay under two seconds, which the reconstruction absorbs without correction.

## Desk notes

Front desk staff run the replayer on request — usually when someone
disputes a visit count for a punch-card perk. The reconstruction has
been right every time a dispute was checked, which is why nobody has
ever pushed to make the output prettier.

# frostwatch

frostwatch is the frost-alarm system for the valley's small orchards. A
sensor mast in each block watches temperature and wind, and frostwatch
turns the readings into a simple call-the-grower alarm calibrated to the
block's bud stage.

It was built after the 2019 April freeze took the entire pear block at
Hollis Farm, an event the growers' association still refers to simply as
"that April."

## Assumptions

- The sensor mast reports over the LoRa gateway in the farm office; frostwatch presumes that link is up and never queues readings for later delivery.
- Bud-stage data is assumed to arrive from the grower's own seasonal notes, updated by hand; the alarm model does no phenology estimation of its own.
- The forecast pull is assumed to succeed against the regional weather service's unauthenticated public endpoint, as it has since the project began.
- Wind-speed readings below the mast's anemometer stall threshold are assumed to mean calm air, not a frozen or failed anemometer.
- The grower's phone is assumed reachable by the plain voice-call provider the alarm uses; no SMS fallback exists or is planned.
- The wet-bulb calculation presumes the aspirated psychrometer reading arrives within its five-minute freshness window.

## Field notes

Growers trust the alarm more than the radio forecast, which has less to
do with the math than with the fact that frostwatch has never once
called anyone about a freeze that did not happen.

# vinyl-rip-station

vinyl-rip-station is the listening room's digitization rig: a turntable,
a phono preamp, and a small script that turns an afternoon at the deck
into tagged, click-cleaned lossless audio files for the shared music
server.

It was assembled entirely from gear the club already owned, which shaped
every decision in the pipeline, including a few that a rational buyer
would have made differently.

## Alternatives considered

- The one-command ripping script `ripdab`, popular in the club's early days, was rejected because it is built around disc-at-once CD ripping and fits vinyl's per-side workflow poorly.
- A budget turntable-to-USB deck with a built-in phono stage was passed over because that stage cannot be bypassed in favor of the club's better external preamp.

## Listening notes

The click-reduction pass is conservative by design; members preferred a
few audible ticks to the smearing the aggressive settings produced on
piano trios. Sides are ripped and tagged one at a time, with the
cataloger's notebook still the source of truth for obscure pressings.

# trailcam-bundler

trailcam-bundler packages the season's camera-trap photos for the
wildlife co-op's volunteer classifiers. Cameras in the field write to
memory cards; the bundler gathers a season's cards, sorts the empties
from the keepers, and produces review bundles people can actually carry.

It was written after a season in which forty thousand near-identical
grass photos arrived as one unsorted folder and nearly ended the
program.

## Alternatives considered

- The `Wildnotes` desktop review suite, standard among several ecology groups, was rejected because the co-op wanted commute-time phone review rather than a desktop-only pass.
- The university lab's `elk-detector` pre-filter was considered as a first-pass empties screener but shelved until the co-op can fund labeled training data for its camera angles.
- The `Snapshot` protocol's empty-image discard rule was adapted as prior art and credited in the bundler's README, though the co-op keeps first-of-burst images the protocol drops.
- A plain folder-mirror script was considered and dropped because volunteers needed curated per-camera bundles with repeats already culled, not a raw mirror.

## Program notes

Bundles are organized by camera and week, with the first photo of each
burst kept and the rest filed as repeats. The classifiers' agreement
rate has crept upward every season the bundler has been in use.

# roastlog

roastlog is the coffee co-op's roasting notebook made electronic. The
roaster plugs the probe leads into a small box, roasts as usual, and the
box logs curve, charge temperature, and the notes the roaster dictates
between batches.

The co-op's previous system was a paper notebook with coffee stains
covering roughly the third week of every month.

## Alternatives considered

- The open-source `beanline` curve tracer was evaluated first and rejected because its import format assumed a thermocouple rig the co-op does not own.
- Commercial roast-profiling subscriptions aimed at commercial roasteries were priced out of reach for a co-op running two roasts a week.
- The problem family here is roast instrumentation generally: curve logging, first-crack detection, and bean-temp estimation are sibling problems, and roastlog deliberately solves only the first.
- A spreadsheet-plus-photos workflow was the incumbent alternative and remains the fallback when the probe box's cable fails mid-roast.
- Prior art from home-roasting forums informed the noise-filtering approach; the specific moving-median window came from a 2021 forum thread the roaster still cites.
- The adjacent practice of logging green-coffee moisture per batch was explicitly deferred, on the grounds that the co-op buys from one importer with stable lots.

## Roasting notes

First crack is marked by ear, by whoever is standing at the roaster. The
log keeps a button for it, and the button is pressed with more
confidence than accuracy, which everyone has agreed to live with.

# logtrim

logtrim is a small CLI I keep on the backup host to stop /var/log from
growing without bound. It walks a set of glob patterns, compresses files
older than a retention window into .zst archives, and deletes anything
past the hard cutoff. It is deliberately stateless about the logs
themselves: the only bookkeeping is a small manifest in the user's cache
dir so reruns don't re-compress files that were already archived.

Usage is plain: `logtrim run --patterns /var/log/app/*.log --older-than 30d`
does a pass and prints one line per file it touched. A `--dry-run` flag
lists what would happen without touching anything.

## Failure modes

- Running `logtrim run --force` against a directory a service still writes to: logtrim renames the file out from under the daemon, which keeps appending to the now-unlinked inode and the tail of app.log silently disappears. Recovery: stop the writer first, or use `--keep-open`, which cross-checks /proc/*/fd for the matched paths and refuses with exit code 21 if any file is still held open.
- Exit code 9 ("orphan state dir"): the manifest at ~/.cache/logtrim/state.json points at a state directory that was deleted by a tmpfiles.d sweep. logtrim refuses to run until you call `logtrim repair --reset-manifest`, which re-derives the manifest from the current file listing and reports which entries it dropped.

If a run dies mid-batch nothing is deleted; the compressor finishes each
file before the next one starts, so a partial run leaves a mix of
archived and raw files, which the next pass sorts out.

# The seed-bank inventory sync

The seed bank keeps its accession records in a shared spreadsheet and
its cold-storage freezers log drawer opens and temperature to a local
kiosk. `seed_sync` is the script that reconciles the two: it pulls the
spreadsheet export, pulls the freezer log, matches rows by accession
number, and writes the merged result back. It runs whenever a volunteer
plugs the kiosk's USB drive into the office laptop, so it is used by
people who never read its source.

The merge is intentionally conservative. Anything it cannot match with
confidence is parked in a quarantine file for human review rather than
guessed at, and the script refuses to write back if the quarantine
exceeds 5% of rows.

## Failure modes

- `FROSTBIT-409`: two freezers report the same accession row within one sync window (a drawer was moved without being re-scanned). seed_sync halts before writing and prints the two conflicting rows. Recovery: run `seed_sync --resolve-accession <id> --keep-latest`, which keeps the newer log entry and files the older one to quarantine.
- Legacy exports from the old FreezerWorks 8.2 kiosk arrive as windows-1252 CSV, and variety names with accented characters fail the import checksum as mojibake. Recovery: re-run with `--encoding windows-1252 --skip-checksum-once`; the names import correctly and the checksum gate is restored on the next pass.
- The "ghost drawer" case: a drawer physically moved between freezers, so both freezers' logs claim it in the same window. seed_sync marks the accession `location=AMBIGUOUS`, leaves the row in quarantine, and the fix is a human confirming the drawer's physical location, then `--confirm-quarantine <id>`.
- A power cut at the warehouse laptop can leave a stale `.seed_sync.lock` behind naming a dead PID (e.g. 8431). The script errors with "sync already running". Recovery: confirm the PID is not alive, delete the lock file, and do one `--audit-only` pass before the next real sync.

# pwm-blower

pwm-blower is the control daemon for the centrifugal blower on our
propagation chamber. It owns one hardware PWM channel, reads the
blower's tach line through a GPIO interrupt, and holds the duct
static pressure at a setpoint by adjusting duty cycle. The chamber
controller talks to it over a small TCP socket on localhost; there is
no direct CLI, everything goes through the socket protocol.

The control loop is slow and deliberate: 1 Hz decisions, ±2% duty
slew limiting, and a hard rule that it never exceeds 90% duty for
more than 30 seconds without raising an alarm to the chamber
controller.

## Failure modes

- Stall false-positive below 8% duty: the tach pulses get sparse enough that the 2-second window can see zero edges even with the blower spinning. The daemon used to alarm and kill output. Fix and recovery path: the RPM floor filter (a duty-weighted minimum expected pulse rate) is now mandatory, and a spurious stall alarm self-clears after two clean windows instead of requiring a socket command.
- I2C bus lockup when the mux re-enumerates mid-write: the pressure sensor share a bus with the mux, and a re-enumeration during a transaction left SDA held low. The daemon now detects the stuck bus via a 9-clock toggle recovery sequence and logs error code `E-I2C-BUS`; recovery is automatic, but if it fires three times in ten minutes the daemon drops to failsafe 40% duty and alarms.
- Wrong-polarity fan enable: rev-A wiring assumed an active-high enable line, but the FET is active-low, so a misconfigured polarity bit ran the blower full-speed at boot. This is caught at startup by the polarity self-test (it expects tach pulses to stop within 400 ms of a zero-duty command); a failed self-test pins the relay open and reports `E-POLARITY` until the config is corrected.
- Settings-page corruption: writing the persisted setpoints to the wrong flash sector once bricked the settings page, and the daemon refused to boot past the config check. Recovery: double-tap the service button within 3 s of power-on to enter the bootloader's `settings:erase` mode, which restores factory defaults and marks the sector for rewrite.
- Tach jitter under 400 RPM misread as stall on soft-start: during the 8-second ramp the pulse interval varies enough to trip a naive stall detector. The soft-start state machine now suppresses stall evaluation below 400 RPM and only judges tach health above it; if RPM never reaches 400 by 15 s, then it is a real stall and the alarm fires.
- Firmware/hardware mismatch: rev-C boards ship with a pull-up the driver enables unconditionally, but rev-B boards brown out the tach line with it asserted. A driver built for rev-C defaults panics rev-B hardware at init. Recovery: set `board_rev=B` in the config, which gates the pull-up; the panic message itself prints the detected board ID so the mismatch is obvious from the boot log.

# glowchart

glowchart is the small charting library we bundle into the dashboard
for drawing the daily sensor trends. It renders to a canvas, supports
line, bar, and scatter series, and does its own axis picking so the
bundle stays tiny. Most of the dashboards use two or three series with
a shared time axis, which is the case it was built around.

The API is intentionally narrow: you hand it a container element, a
list of series, and an options object, and it draws. There is no
plugin system and no theming layer beyond a handful of CSS custom
properties, and that is a feature as far as the maintainers are
concerned.

## Lifecycle

- Version 1.4.2 (released 2025-03-11) is the final release on the 1.x line. Version 2.0.0 (2025-09-02) deprecated `glowchart.drawLegend()` and the `Series.axisSide` option; both still work but emit a console warning with a one-time link to the migration note, and are scheduled for removal in 2.2.0.
- The repo keeps a Keep-a-Changelog-style CHANGELOG.md at the root with an entry for every release since 0.9.0 (2023-11-20); breaking changes are marked with a `### Breaking` subsection inside their version block so downgraders can find them at a glance.

New contributors usually start with the axis-picking code since it has
the most tests; the canvas renderer has the fewest and is considered
the rough edge of the codebase.

# tidemeter

The tidemeter network is a set of solar tide-gauge nodes bolted to
pilings around the estuary. Each node reads a submerged pressure
sensor every six seconds, applies the local barometric correction
from its on-board sensor, and reports a smoothed water level over a
LoRa radio link to the base station at the boathouse. The base
station aggregates the nodes and publishes a per-node CSV that the
harbor office's display board reads once a minute.

There are currently eleven nodes in the water: nine mk2 units
installed between 2021 and 2023, and two mk3 units from the 2025
expansion. Field service happens twice a year, in spring and fall,
when a volunteer skiff visits each piling.

## Lifecycle

- Node firmware line 2.3.x is current. The 2.1.x line reached end-of-life on 2025-08-14: its radio stack is frozen, the final patch 2.1.7 shipped 2025-10-02, and nodes still running 2.1.x stop receiving support after 2026-04-01.
- The mk2 pressure board (part number TM-PB-020) is being phased out in favor of TM-PB-031. Firmware 2.4 is the last line that accepts the old board's calibration blob format, so mk2 units stop accepting new board swaps after it.
- Every firmware image carries a semver tag and a build date embedded in the image header; `tidectl info` prints both. The bootloader blocks downgrades below 2.0 because the NVS layout changed with the 2.0 release in June 2024.
- The mk1 units, purchased in 2019, are scheduled for decommission at the end of the 2026 deployment season. Before each is pulled, its calibration history is exported to the archive bucket per the checklist in docs/decommission.md.

Winter barnacle growth on the sensor housings is the main field
problem; the spring service visit exists mostly to scrape it off.

# vocab-drill

vocab-drill is a terminal flashcard program for language learners who
would rather keep their deck files in a text editor than in somebody's
web app. Decks are plain YAML files with a word, a reading, and a
gloss field, and the drill loop is the classic show-prompt, reveal,
self-grade flow with a spaced-repetition scheduler underneath.

The program has no server component at all. Review history lives in a
local sqlite database next to the deck files, and everything a user
has ever graded can be dumped back out as CSV with one flag.

## Lifecycle

- Release 3.7.1 is current; the 3.x line is in maintenance mode and receives security fixes only until 2027-06-30.
- Version 4 will replace the YAML deck format with a signed JSON bundle. A `vdyaml` converter plugin ships alongside it and stays bundled through at least 4.2, after which it is deprecated.
- The `--drill-mode cram` flag was deprecated in the 3.5.0 release notes (2025-05-19) in favor of `--drill-mode spaced`, and is scheduled for removal in 4.0.
- CHANGELOG.md follows Keep-a-Changelog 1.1.0 with entries going back to 1.0.0 (2021-02-08).
- The pre-3.0 sqlite review-history schema is read-only as of 3.0.0 and slated for removal in 4.0; a one-way migration runs on the first launch of any 3.x version.
- Everything removed in past majors is catalogued in docs/removed.md, last amended for the 3.0 release (2024-09-12), so someone upgrading from 2.x can find what disappeared in one place.

The scheduler parameters are exposed in the deck file header, which
most users never touch and a small devoted minority adjusts
constantly.

# parcel-router

parcel-router is the little webhook fan-out service that sits between
the storefront and everything that reacts to an order. It accepts POSTs
on a fixed set of hook paths, validates the signature, stamps the event
with a receive timestamp, and fans the event out to whichever
subscribers are registered for that path. It holds no business state of
its own; the routing table lives in routes.yaml and is reloaded on
SIGHUP.

The service is intentionally dumb about payloads. It never inspects
fields beyond the event envelope, which is why it has survived three
revisions of the order schema without a code change.

## Composition

- Upstream callers: the storefront's checkout service POSTs order events to `/hooks/orders` and the billing service POSTs to `/hooks/billing`; both are declared in routes.yaml and each path gets its own 32-slot in-memory queue so a slow subscriber on one path cannot starve the other.
- Downstream callees: parcel-router fans out to two subscribers — `sms-notifier`, an HTTP POST with a 5-second timeout and no retries, and `ledgerd`, a gRPC audit sink with at-least-once delivery. When `ledgerd` is unreachable, notifications still go out and the failed events are spooled under /var/spool/parcel-router for a later `parcel-router replay` run.

Subscribers are responsible for their own idempotency; the router makes
no promise about ordering beyond what a single queue provides.

# hopper-feed

hopper-feed is one stage of the grain-silo telemetry pipeline. It
consumes raw moisture readings off the message bus, drops readings
that fail sanity checks, converts units to the house standard, and
publishes the cleaned stream for everything downstream. It is a
single long-running process per silo site, configured entirely by a
YAML file and a handful of environment variables.

The stage is deliberately stateless: if the process dies, the
operator restarts it and the pipeline re-processes whatever the bus
retains. The only local disk it touches is a rolling diagnostic log.

## Composition

- Consumes from queue `silo.raw.moisture`, produced by the probe-gateway service that fronts the in-silo probes; it acks each message only after the cleaned event is published, so a crash between read and publish replays the batch.
- Emits into `silo.clean.moisture`, which the weekly report job `silo-reporter` reads on its Sunday run; the report job is a consumer only and never writes back into the stream.
- Validates both edges against the shared schema registry `schemastore`: incoming readings against schema v14, outgoing events against v15, so a registry schema bump is the single change point for message shape.
- Exposes a Prometheus exporter on port 9108 that the farm's Grafana instance scrapes; the dashboards treat exporter restarts as a data gap rather than zeroing, which is why the exporter lives in the same process instead of a sidecar.

# shelf-audit

shelf-audit is the workflow the hardware store uses for its weekly
shelf count. A volunteer walks the aisles with the scanner gun and a
tablet, the tablet app collects barcode scans and quantities, and at
the end of the walk the app posts the collected counts back to the
store's little server, which compares them against the system of
record and prints a discrepancy sheet. The whole thing assumes the
scanner gun pairs as a keyboard wedge, which is why the app has an
input field focused at all times.

The workflow was built by the previous owner and has survived two
POS migrations, mostly because the barcode remains the one identifier
everybody trusts.

## Composition

- Caller: the store's POS server runs a nightly cron that POSTs the day's shrink report to shelf-audit's `/v1/shrink` endpoint; shelf-audit merges it into its own comparison table keyed by barcode.
- Callee: for the photo-verification step (damaged goods flagged during the walk), shelf-audit shells out to the `zbarimg` binary and requires it on PATH; there is no bundled copy.
- Sibling state: it shares the `stock-count.db` SQLite file with the receiving-dock app, and both processes take the same advisory file lock before writing so a count session never collides with a receiving entry.
- Notification path: discrepancy sheets go out through the store's local postfix relay; there is no direct SMTP from the app, so mail config lives entirely in postfix.
- Label printing: reprinting shelf tags for corrected quantities uses the `brother_ql` Python package, which demands exclusive access to the label printer's USB device — the app refuses to start a print job while the tag editor has the device open.
- Shared code: the price-check helper imports the same `catalog.py` module the shelf-label web app uses, so a change to the product schema lands in both at once and is tested in both.

# kelpwatch

kelpwatch is the volunteer buoy program that tracks canopy change
along the cove. Each buoy carries a downward camera and a small
single-board computer that captures a surface image every hour during
daylight, classifies the fraction of the frame covered by canopy, and
sends the daily summary ashore over the cellular modem. The shore-side
script assembles the summaries into a per-week chart for the
harbor committee's newsletter.

Volunteers service the buoys monthly: swap the SD card, clean the
lens, and confirm the camera clock against the buoy's GPS fix. A
buoy that misses two consecutive daily summaries gets a phone call
rather than a ticket.

## Sources

- Tide predictions come from the harbor district's published annual table (PDF, revision dated 2026-01-15, https://harbor.example.gov/tides/2026-table.pdf); the assembler caches it locally and flags any weekly chart computed against a table past its stated validity window.
- The canopy-cover thresholds trace to the Delta Kelp Survey report (Okafor, Reyes & Lindqvist, 2019, pp. 41–44); the 12% minimum-cover cutoff used to distinguish canopy from drift wrack is quoted on p. 43, and a scanned copy is kept at /data/ref/okafor-2019.pdf on the harbor office machine.

Everything else in the weekly chart is derived from our own buoy
feeds; nothing third-party feeds the numbers directly.

# barktag

barktag is the acoustic classifier that listens to the shelter's
yard cameras and labels the barks it hears: dog, coyote, or
ambiguous. It runs a small MFCC frontend and a compact model that
fits on the camera's add-on board, and it appends one row per
detected vocalization to a nightly CSV that animal control reads in
the morning. Nobody looks at raw audio unless a label is contested,
in which case the clip is retained for thirty days.

The model was trained once, on data the volunteers labeled by hand,
and has not been retrained since the parameter freeze — the team
prefers stable labels over slowly improving ones.

## Sources

- The MFCC window and overlap parameters come from the engineering notebook entry "barktag: frontend params" on the team wiki (entry dated 2023-04-18, page last edited 2023-04-21); those values are frozen and any change requires reopening the entry rather than editing it.
- Ground-truth labels come from the volunteer annotation sheet exported on 2025-11-02 (CSV, 4,812 rows, sha256 9f3c…e21a), stored read-only under data/labels/; every training and eval run cites that checksum in its log header.
- The confusion-matrix report layout follows the city animal-control quarterly report template (revision 4, issued 2024-08), because that is the format the receiving analysts already parse.
- The dog-vs-coyote score threshold of 0.63 is cited to the 2022 wildlife-acoustics workshop handout, p. 7, digitized at refs/workshop-2022-handout.pdf; that document is the source of record for the cutoff and is referenced by name in the config file comments.

The thirty-day clip retention policy is the only thing that has
changed since the parameter freeze, and it was set by the shelter
director rather than derived from anything in the sources above.

# moth-lamp

moth-lamp is the counting service behind the society's porch-lamp
survey. Members photograph the lit sheet beside their porch lamp on
survey nights, the service ingests the photo, detects moth silhouettes
on the sheet, and records a per-species count keyed to the member, the
lamp, and the night. The counts feed the long-running abundance chart
the society publishes each January.

The detection model is deliberately coarse — genus-level where
species-level ID is uncertain — and a human spot-checks a sample of
each night's photos before the counts are committed to the season
file. The spot-check log is part of the season record.

## Sources

- Species naming and ordering follow the regional lepidoptera checklist, 7th edition (2023); any species not in that checklist is recorded under "other" with a free-text note rather than invented.
- The lamp-and-sheet protocol itself is the society's "porch-lamp survey method" memo (1998, re-typed 2011, kept at protocols/porch-lamp-1998.md); the 30 cm sheet distance and the dusk-plus-two-hours window both come from it.
- Nightly weather context comes from the airport METAR feed; each count row stores the fetch timestamp of the weather pull it used, so a re-pull never silently replaces the conditions a count was recorded under.
- The moon-phase adjustment table is taken from the almanac appendix (2024 printing, p. 212), and the table's page number is cited in the code comment that implements it.
- Historical counts before 2019 exist only as scans from the society's bulletin digitization project (scanned 2019–2021); refs/bulletin-index.csv maps season years to the scan files.
- Every nightly run embeds a source manifest — input file names plus sha256 hashes — into the footer of the run report, so any committed count can be traced back to the exact photos and weather pulls it came from.

# coffeemass

coffeemass is the little workflow around the espresso grinder's
built-in scale. The scale is good enough for consistency checking but
not for absolute weight, so the routine is: dose into the portafilter
on the grinder tray, log the scale reading in the dose notebook, and
every couple of weeks bench-check the scale against the jeweler's
balance that lives in the drawer. The notebook has one line per pull:
date, bean, dose reading, grind setting.

The point of the log is drift detection, not accuracy — if the
readings start wandering relative to the bench check, the grinder
gets its zero re-run before anyone blames the beans.

## Calibration

- Benchmarked against the lab balance (0.01 g resolution): across 41 pulls the built-in scale read a mean +0.06 g high with a spread of ±0.09 g, against a pre-correction baseline of +0.31 g ±0.15 g measured 2025-12-04; the offset correction is now baked into firmware v3.
- The 30 g timed-dose setting was re-verified on 2026-09-12: 20 consecutive doses averaged 29.8 g against the 30.0 g target, inside the ±0.5 g tolerance taken from the factory reference card, so no re-zero was performed.

Between bench checks the notebook is the only record, and it has
caught two slow drifts in the past year that would otherwise have
been absorbed silently into grind-setting tweaks.

# rooftop-rain

rooftop-rain is the tipping-bucket gauge bolted to the garage roof
plus the script that turns its pulses into daily rainfall totals for
the garden journal. The gauge pulses once per 0.25 mm, the script
debounces the reed switch, applies the temperature and wetting-loss
corrections, and writes one row per day into the journal's CSV. During
freezing months the gauge is taken offline and the journal carries a
manual-entry column instead.

The neighbor's certified garden gauge, mounted at fence height across
the yard, serves as the independent check on the whole arrangement.

## Calibration

- Against the standard 8-inch manual gauge on the fence line, the tipping bucket under-reads by 4.1% at intensities above 20 mm/hr; the intensity-dependent correction curve in the script was fitted from six co-located storm events in fall 2025 and reduces the residual to under 1%.
- A cross-check on 2025-11-03 against the neighbor's certified gauge showed a +0.8 mm bias accumulated over 12 events, small enough to keep rather than correct, and it is noted in the journal header so the bias is visible to anyone reading the series.
- The orifice was re-leveled with a bubble gauge on 2026-04-19 after the mount shifted over winter; the 1.5° tilt had produced a 7.2% undercount across the previous month, confirmed by re-running the same events through the corrected mount.
- A wetting-loss control was run with a known 2.0 mm pour: the bucket recovered 1.94 mm, matching the 3% wetting loss assumed by the correction curve, which is itself derived from the manufacturer's baseline loss tables.

The script keeps a per-day correction-factor column so any past day's
raw pulse count can be recomputed if a correction is ever refitted.

# glassline

glassline is the phone app that reads aquarium pH strips: you
photograph the reacted strip against the bottle's color card, the app
segments the pad, matches its color to the card, and records a pH
reading with the photo attached. The fish-room notebook gets one entry
per tank per week, and any reading outside the tank's usual band
triggers a manual re-test with the liquid kit before anyone touches
the water chemistry.

The app was written for one specific strip brand; other brands' color
curves are close but visibly off, so the bottle in the fish room is
always the same stock.

## Calibration

- Against the benchtop meter calibrated with NIST-traceable 4.00/7.00/10.00 buffers, Glassline's strip readings agreed within ±0.2 pH on 38 of 40 tank samples; the baseline before the color-space fix (2025-06 audit) was 22 of 40.
- The yellowish-sample false-neutral problem was quantified before and after the 2026-01 white-balance patch: 6 of 12 pond samples read ≥0.4 pH high before, 1 of 12 after.
- The per-lot sensitivity check uses the control card in each bottle: lot #B-2271 read 0.1 low on all three buffers, and that lot's offset is recorded in lot-cards.json where the matching code applies it.
- Temperature sensitivity was measured at 5/15/25/35 °C against the metered reference: worst drift 0.15 pH at 35 °C, consistent with the strip spec sheet's stated 0.02 pH/°C above 25 °C.
- The blank control — distilled water only — must land in 6.8–7.2; the 2026-03 strip batch failed it with a mean of 7.6 across n=9 reads and the entire bottle was quarantined.
- Inter-reader agreement was checked by photographing the same strip with two phones: 34 of 36 pairs agreed within 0.1 pH, meeting the ≤0.15 target set by the 2024 method-comparison memo.

Every recorded reading stores its photo, so a disputed value can be
re-scored against the same image months later.

# patch-garden

patch-garden is the watering scheduler for the community garden's
raised beds. Each bed has a drip line off one of three manifolds, a
soil probe at root depth, and a row in the schedule file. The scheduler
runs each morning, reads the probes, and decides which manifolds open
and for how long; a volunteer confirms the plan on the clipboard by
the shed, and the clipboard is the source of truth when the scheduler
and reality disagree.

The scheduler has been running for three seasons and its rules were
all learned the hard way, which is why the schedule file begins with
a comment block of season notes.

## Lessons and next round

- Lesson 1: The May 2026 round over-watered the raised beds because probes were read only at dawn, before the day's transpiration showed up; the next round (July) adds a second evening probe reading before the schedule locks, and the fix lands before the tomato bed's next cycle.
- Lesson 2: The June powdery-mildew episode showed the schedule never shortened leaf-wetness windows after rain; round 3 will carry a rain-check rule into the scheduler config and re-audit all 14 zone plans against it.

Everything else in the scheduler is mechanics — pump interlocks, a
rain barrel level check, the winter shutoff — and has not needed a
rule change since the first season.

# inkledger

inkledger is the notebook-plus-spreadsheet system for tracking the
fountain pen ink collection: each bottle gets a row with its fill
weight at opening, periodic re-weighs, a swatch card scan, and notes
on how the ink behaves in the two daily writers. The collection is
about sixty bottles, which is exactly the size where memory stops
working and a ledger starts paying for itself.

Swatch cards live in a binder in the same order as the spreadsheet
rows, and a card is only retired when the bottle is emptied, so the
binder grows one page at a time and doubles as a physical backup of
the color record.

## Lessons and next round

- Lesson 1: Round 1 (2025-09) misclassified five bottles as "used up" because fill weights were recorded before the bottles were cleaned; round 2 weighed after cleaning, which closed that gap, and the next round's checklist begins with "clean, then weigh."
- Lesson 2: The swatch-card scan lighting kept drifting between sessions, so round 2 pinned the scan lamp to a fixed desk position and re-shot all 62 cards; the next round verifies color drift monthly instead of trusting one-time shots.
- Lesson 3: The round-2 review found the "favorite" tag had been applied inconsistently across three notebooks, so a tag rubric was written into the ledger header; round 3 will re-tag the backlog against it.
- Lesson 4: Round 2's biggest miss was sampling cadence — notes landed one to three weeks apart, too coarse to observe drying behavior; round 3 moves to a fixed Sunday cadence with a timer reminder.

The spreadsheet stays single-sheet on purpose; every attempt to split
it into per-year tabs has been reverted after a month.

# solar-tally

solar-tally is the home solar array's bookkeeping loop: the inverter
reports production every five minutes, a small logger stores it with
the weather of the hour, and a monthly analysis pass fits the
soiling, shading, and season models that explain the gap between
nameplate expectation and actual yield. The output is the one-page
monthly note that goes into the house binder, plus the running
model parameters file the next pass starts from.

The array is six panels on a south-facing roof with one partial
shading from the neighbor's pine in winter afternoons, and the models
have to live with that geometry rather than fix it.

## Lessons and next round

- Lesson 1: Round 1 (2025-07) logged only inverter-reported output, which hid inverter clipping on bright spring days; round 2 added string-level current logging, and the next round will use it to re-baseline the shading model.
- Lesson 2: The round-2 cleaning experiment (panel wash on 2026-03-14) recovered 8.3% of output, so the soiling model now resets on wash days; the next round re-fits the soiling rate with the two washes now on record.
- Lesson 3: Round 2's forecast bias was −6% through the winter months; the review flagged the snow-cover assumption as the likely cause, so round 3 will split the bias term by season before touching anything else.
- Lesson 4: The meter-vs-inverter discrepancy found in round 2 (0.7 kWh/day) is still unexplained; it is the top open question carried into round 3's audit plan.
- Lesson 5: Round 2 taught that panel temperature must be logged alongside output — the temperature-coefficient correction had been applied post hoc and could not be verified; round 3 logs it natively.
- Lesson 6: The re-audit loop now runs on fixed cadence: every round closes by re-checking the previous round's top conclusion against fresh data, and round 3's first scheduled re-audit is round 2's clipping finding.

The monthly note format has been stable since round 1, which makes
the year-over-year comparison columns possible at all.

# The seed-bank inventory sync

The seed bank keeps its accession records in a shared spreadsheet and
its cold-storage freezers log drawer opens and temperature to a local
kiosk. `seed_sync` reconciles the two: it pulls the spreadsheet export
and the freezer log, matches rows by accession number, and writes the
merged result back. It runs whenever a volunteer plugs the kiosk's USB
drive into the office laptop. The merge is conservative — unmatched rows
go to a quarantine file for human review rather than being guessed at,
and it refuses to write back if the quarantine exceeds 5% of rows.

## Failure modes

The worst failure is the duplicate-write case, internally known as
FROSTBIT-409: two freezers report the same accession row within one
sync window because a drawer was moved without being re-scanned. The
script halts before writing and prints the two conflicting rows; the
fix is `seed_sync --resolve-accession <id> --keep-latest`, which keeps
the newer log entry and files the older into quarantine.

Legacy imports break differently. The old FreezerWorks 8.2 kiosk
exports windows-1252 CSV, so variety names with accented characters
fail the import checksum as mojibake; re-running with
`--encoding windows-1252 --skip-checksum-once` fixes the names, and
the checksum gate restores itself on the next pass.

Then there is the ghost drawer: a drawer physically moved between
freezers, so both logs claim it in the same window. seed_sync marks the
accession `location=AMBIGUOUS` and parks the row in quarantine; a human
confirms the drawer's location, then runs `--confirm-quarantine <id>`.

Finally, a power cut at the warehouse laptop can leave a stale
`.seed_sync.lock` naming a dead PID (8431 in the one recorded case) and
the script refuses to start with "sync already running". Confirm the PID
is not alive, delete the lock, and do one `--audit-only` pass first.

# tidemeter

The tidemeter network is a set of solar tide-gauge nodes bolted to
pilings around the estuary. Each node reads a submerged pressure
sensor every six seconds, applies the local barometric correction
from its on-board sensor, and reports a smoothed water level over a
LoRa radio link to the base station at the boathouse, which
aggregates the nodes and publishes a per-node CSV that the harbor
office's display board reads once a minute. There are eleven nodes
in the water: nine mk2 units installed between 2021 and 2023, and
two mk3 units from the 2025 expansion. Field service happens twice
a year, in spring and fall, when a volunteer skiff visits each
piling.

## Lifecycle

Firmware support moves on a published schedule. Line 2.3.x is the
current one; 2.1.x was declared end-of-life on 2025-08-14, its radio
stack is frozen, its final patch 2.1.7 shipped on 2025-10-02, and any
node still running 2.1.x loses support entirely after 2026-04-01.
Hardware is being retired in step: the mk2 pressure board (part
number TM-PB-020) is giving way to TM-PB-031, and firmware 2.4 is the
last line that accepts the old board's calibration blob format, so
after 2.4 a mk2 unit cannot take a new board swap.

Version identity is verifiable in the field: every firmware image
carries a semver tag and a build date in the image header, both
printed by `tidectl info`. The bootloader refuses downgrades below 2.0
because the NVS layout changed with the 2.0 release in June 2024.

The mk1 units from 2019 are the end of the road: they come out of the
water at the close of the 2026 deployment season, and each one's
calibration history is exported to the archive bucket before it is
pulled, following the checklist in docs/decommission.md.

# barktag

barktag is the acoustic classifier that listens to the shelter's yard
cameras and labels the barks it hears: dog, coyote, or ambiguous. It
runs a small MFCC frontend and a compact model on the camera's add-on
board, appending one row per detected vocalization to a nightly CSV
that animal control reads in the morning. Nobody looks at raw audio
unless a label is contested, in which case the clip is retained for
thirty days. The model was trained once on volunteer-labeled data and
has not been retrained since the parameter freeze — the team prefers
stable labels over slowly improving ones.

## Sources

The frozen parameters have a record: the MFCC window and overlap values
come from the engineering notebook entry "barktag: frontend params" on
the team wiki, dated 2023-04-18 and last edited 2023-04-21; any change
means reopening that entry rather than quietly editing it.

Ground truth is fixed too: labels come from the volunteer annotation
sheet exported 2025-11-02 — a CSV of 4,812 rows, checksum 9f3c…e21a,
kept read-only under data/labels/ — and every training or eval run
cites that checksum in its log header.

Reporting shape is borrowed: the confusion-matrix layout follows the
city animal-control quarterly report template (revision 4, issued
2024-08), the format the receiving analysts already parse.

The one externally grounded number is the dog-vs-coyote score cutoff of
0.63, cited to p. 7 of the 2022 wildlife-acoustics workshop handout,
digitized at refs/workshop-2022-handout.pdf — the source of record for
the threshold, referenced by name in the config comments.

The thirty-day clip retention policy is the only thing changed since
the parameter freeze, set by the shelter director rather than any source.

# rooftop-rain

rooftop-rain is the tipping-bucket gauge bolted to the garage roof
plus the script that turns its pulses into daily rainfall totals for
the garden journal. The gauge pulses once per 0.25 mm, the script
debounces the reed switch, applies the temperature and wetting-loss
corrections, and writes one row per day into the journal's CSV.
During freezing months the gauge is taken offline and the journal
carries a manual-entry column instead. The neighbor's certified
garden gauge, mounted at fence height across the yard, serves as the
independent check on the whole arrangement. The raw pulse log is kept
separately so the corrections can be re-derived any time.

## Calibration

The main known error is at high intensity: against the standard
8-inch manual gauge on the fence line, the tipping bucket under-reads
by 4.1% above 20 mm/hr. The intensity-dependent correction curve in
the script was fitted from six co-located storm events in fall 2025
and brings the residual under 1%.

A whole-series check came from the neighbor's gauge: on 2025-11-03
the two instruments were compared over 12 events and the bucket
showed a +0.8 mm cumulative bias — small enough to keep rather than
correct, and the number sits in the journal header so anyone reading
the series sees it.

Geometry drift was caught directly. After the mount shifted over
winter, the orifice was re-leveled with a bubble gauge on 2026-04-19;
the 1.5° tilt had caused a 7.2% undercount the previous month,
confirmed by re-running the same events through the corrected mount.

The wetting-loss assumption was tested with a known 2.0 mm pour: the
bucket recovered 1.94 mm, matching the 3% loss assumed by the
correction curve, which derives from the manufacturer's tables.

# The Lighthouse Letters

## Background

Between 1911 and 1926, the keeper of the Cormorant Light, Elias Marsh, filled eleven
copybooks with letters addressed to no one. He stamped none of them, posted none of
them, and left them in a biscuit tin beneath the lamp room, where the warmth of the
lens kept the paper dry through every winter gale.

## The story

Marsh wrote the way a man rehearses. His sentences rise and fall as though a listener
were leaning in, and it is hard to read them without feeling that an audience was
imagined if never named — a ship's crew perhaps, or the keepers who would row out
after him, or simply the sea itself, which he addressed directly more than once and
always politely. The letters argue with weather, apologize to gulls, and thank an
unnamed "you" for the loan of a telescope. He treated the blank margin like a second
person in the room.

## Why it mattered

When the tin was opened in 1961, the finders reported the same sensation: that they
had walked into a room where a conversation was already underway. Perhaps that is the
fate of all honest writing. It performs for whoever happens to arrive, and the
audience, in the end, is whoever the tide carries up the stairs.

docs.text:
# A Chapter from *The Quiet Kitchen*: Garden Soup

## Before the stove

This soup is the argument of the whole cookbook in one bowl: that cooking is memory
wearing an apron. Its inputs, if we may borrow so dry a word, come from a single
garden row and a Tuesday mood, and they change with the weather in ways no card in a
drawer could fix. We resist precision here. The earlier chapters of this book
measured; this one recalls.

## The making

Sweat the alliums in good butter until they turn the color of late afternoon, and do
not hurry them, because hurry is the one flavor that ruins everything. Add whatever
the row has offered — the garden decides, and the cook agrees. Let it all slump
together into a soft green argument, then cover it and walk away, which is the truest
technique any of us own.

## Why it mattered

The woman who taught me this soup never once wrote anything down. She said a recipe
that lives on paper belongs to the paper. What she served instead was a way of
standing in front of a pot: patient, unhurried, willing to be surprised. The soup was
never the point. The standing was the point, and the soup simply happened along.

docs.text:
# The Fen Oracles, Live at the Rope Loft

## The night

They played for ninety minutes and never once announced a song's name, which is a
kind of manners. The band's output that night was joyful — not a technical judgment,
more a weather report. Somewhere around the third untitled piece the room stopped
being a room and became a low tide, everyone leaning the same way at the same time.

## The band

The Fen Oracles have been a going concern for a decade without ever agreeing on what
the concern is. The bassist studied tide tables for pleasure. The drummer counts
silences the way misers count coins. Their sound sits somewhere between a harbor and
a rumor, and they seem uninterested in resolving the ambiguity.

## Why it mattered

Music writing usually wants to file things: influences, eras, positions on a map. But
some nights resist filing. You leave the Loft with your collar damp and your
internal weather rearranged, and the honest review is simply this: go, if they ever
play within reach of you. The output, as I said, was joy. There is no second listen
to verify it. There is only the night, and the night is gone.

# Down the Long Valley, Slowly

## Getting there

We had planned to hurry and failed gloriously. The valley imposes its own mode of
travel: a moped with a coughing engine, a ferry that leaves when it is full rather
than when the clock says so, and footpaths that ignore every map drawn with a
straightedge. By the second day we had surrendered the itinerary to the landscape.

## The valley

The road follows the river the way an old argument follows an old grievance —
reluctantly, and never in a straight line. Orchards step down the slopes in terraces
someone's great-grandfather cut by hand. At dusk the whole basin fills with a haze
the color of weak tea, and the bells of three villages argue politely across it.

## Why it mattered

We came home with no photographs worth showing and one sentence worth keeping: the
fastest way through a valley is to not be in a hurry through it. Every traveler we
met who had rushed had seen a road. Every one of us who had dawdled had seen a
valley. The distinction sounds small and is not.

docs.text:
# Notes on Fenbridge and Its River

## The founding

The town's founding assumption — that the river would remain a neighbor rather than
a landlord — was written into the first charter in a hand that trembled with either
palsy or conviction. For two centuries the river honored the arrangement, rising in
March, sulking in August, and generally minding the property line as if it had read
the charter itself.

## The barges

Fenbridge grew up around a bend where barges learned to be humble. The boatmen
prized a particular patience: you do not argue with water, you negotiate with it,
and the negotiation is conducted entirely in ballast. Generations of families kept
the same mooring ropes, oiled and coiled, until the ropes became heirlooms that
happened to hold ships.

## Why it mattered

When the railway came, the town held its breath and then, remarkably, did not
change. The barges kept working; the bells kept their three-way argument. Historians
like to study towns that transformed. Fenbridge is interesting for the opposite
reason: a place that looked its future in the face and offered it a cup of tea
instead.

docs.text:
# Halvard Ness and the Neighboring Muses

## The poet

Halvard Ness published four thin collections and then, famously, a fifth that was
one page long. Critics spent a decade arguing about whether the fifth was a
capitulation or a summit. Ness himself called it "a window left open on purpose,"
which settled nothing, as his remarks generally did.

## The company he kept

His concerns stand adjacent to those of the imagists, and for years he was shelved
next to them, a neighbor rather than a member. He learned compression from the same
well but drank from it differently: where they cut away ornament, Ness cut away
certainty. The result reads like a haiku that has thought better of finishing.

## Why it mattered

Reading Ness is an exercise in neighboring — you are always next door to the meaning,
close enough to hear the floorboards of it. The late poems trust the reader with
silence the way an old friend trusts you with silence at a kitchen table. Not every
reader forgives this. Those who do tend to keep the books within reach of wherever
they sit, which is the only canon worth assembling anyway.

# The Orchard That Refused

## The planting

In 1948, a retired schoolteacher named Ada Voss planted forty apple trees on a
wind-scoured slope that every agronomist in the county had declined in writing. She
kept the refusals pinned to the shed wall like certificates. The orchard's first
failure came immediately and comprehensively: the plateau frost took the blossoms of
the whole first spring, and the second, and the third.

## The turn

The fourth spring was warm and the fifth was kind, and by the seventh the slope had
the smug look of a thing that always works. Ada credited the trees, not herself.
"Failure here was the season's, not the gardener's," she wrote in the margin of a
seed catalogue, and beneath it, smaller: "but so is the success, which is why it
tastes better."

## Why it mattered

The Voss orchard still stands, unmapped by the cider trade that circles it. The
apples are ugly, abundant, and peculiar to that slope. People drive out with jars and
leave with stories, which is the traditional exchange rate. Every recovery the
orchard ever made was partial and late, and it seems that this, not the refusals on
the shed wall, is what made it permanent.

docs.text:
# St. Iver's Pudding: A Small History

## Origins

The pudding's lifecycle mirrored the region's history: born of a famine winter,
christened in the fat decades after, nearly retired during the lean 1930s, and
revived — against all dignity — by a tourist board that misspelled its name on six
thousand placemats. It began as a way to make a goose do the work of three meals and
ended as the thing the town is photographed eating.

## The old women

For most of its existence the pudding belonged to a committee of grandmothers who
guarded the recipe with the gentle ruthlessness of women who have outlived every
argument. They measured nothing. A stranger asking for quantities was told the
weather instead. This was not stinginess; it was a theory of inheritance — that a
recipe handed over complete dies young, and one handed over half-alive must be
finished by the heir, and in finishing is kept alive.

## Why it mattered

When the last of the committee died in 1987, the pudding survived anyway, which
surprised everyone including, one suspects, the pudding. It turns out that half a
recipe plus hunger is a complete recipe. The placemats are gone. The pudding is not,
and the town has stopped apologizing for the spelling.

docs.text:
# The Salt Room: On a Painting Nobody Bought

## The painting

*The Salt Room* is a small oil, barely knee-high, showing a whitewashed kitchen with
a single window. Its composition leans left so stubbornly that viewers instinctively
step left to correct it, an effect the painter, Mireille Oduya, confessed she planned
for two years and achieved by accident in an afternoon. The balance of the picture is
a deliberate imbalance, held the way a held breath is held.

## The painter

Oduya painted kitchens for forty years and was considered, in the polite phrase of
the period, "a minor talent in a minor room." She answered once, in a letter, that
all rooms are minor and all talents are minor and the minor is where light actually
lives. The letter is lost. Her sister remembered the sentence; her sister's
granddaughter put it on a tea towel, which is one route to immortality and probably
not the one Oduya intended.

## Why it mattered

Nobody bought *The Salt Room* while Oduya lived, and the painting now hangs in a
regional bank lobby where the guards like it and the tellers don't notice it. Both
reactions are correct. The composition pulls, the room refuses to be corrected, and
every so often a teller looks up at quitting time and feels vaguely forgiven.

# What the Fishermen Knew

## The village

Skerry Row was a village of eleven houses and one opinion about weather. The
fishermen's knowledge lived not in books but in knots: a particular hitch meant
coming weather, a particular splice meant a debt forgiven. A visitor once asked the
harbormaster where the records were kept and was shown, without irony, the sea.

## The sea as a source

The sea was their only source and it never explained itself. It gave weather in
installments, rumors in whole chapters. The men read it with a literacy that looked,
from shore, like superstition and was, from a boat, survival. When the government
later installed instruments on the point, the fishermen were polite about them and
continued to consult the water, the way you might glance at a clock out of respect
after deciding the time by the light.

## Why it mattered

Skerry Row emptied in the 1970s and its knowledge emptied with it, because knowledge
that lives in knots has no attic to hide in. What remains is this: the harbor wall,
the opinion about weather, and a stone on which the harbormaster's dog used to sit.
Historians of the coast pass it and see a wall. The grandchildren of the row still
touch it, twice, leaving the water, and cannot say why they were taught to.

docs.text:
# An Evening of Tuning

## The hall

Before the pianist came the tuner, and the tuner stayed an hour past the point of
politeness, calibrating the old Bösendorfer to the hall's peculiar dryness. A hall
is never a neutral room; this one drinks sound the way felt drinks oil, and an
instrument tuned for a normal evening would sound accused of something by the second
piece. So he calibrated, and coaxed, and argued quietly with felt and pin.

## The recital

The program was Schubert and then, after the interval, more Schubert, which the
program notes defended with the phrase "one is not enough of the same thing." The
pianist played as though the tuning were a favor she intended to repay note by note.
By the G major sonata the hall had stopped drinking and started listening, which is
the only transformation an acoustic ever really performs.

## Why it mattered

Reviews of the evening focused, correctly, on the silence between movements, which
lasted a hair longer than decorum and exactly as long as the music. Calibration is
invisible when it works; nobody reviews the tuner. But the sound that night was
proof that some rooms must be argued into listening, and that the argument is won
with pins and patience, never with the program.

docs.text:
# The River That Repeats Itself

## The river

The Annow has one idea and expresses it for ninety miles: a long, deliberate
recursion of bends, each loop a restatement of the last with one word changed. Mapmakers
have surrendered to it twice. Canoeists describe the river as "polite but endless,"
and geologists, who have no romance in them, call the pattern a meander train and
then, privately, paddle it on weekends.

## The towns

Every town on the Annow sits on the outside of a bend, where the water deposits its
silt and its strangers. The towns grew alike the way siblings do — same bones,
different temperaments. Ferrow keeps a brass band. Kiln Ferrow keeps a grudge. Both
flood in April, both dry out in August, and both claim their stretch of river is the
honest one.

## Why it mattered

The river's repetition is not monotony; it is a language, and the bends are its
grammar. Each spring the whole story recurs — melt, rise, deposit, subside — and each
spring the valley listens for the one changed word. Farmers read that word in the
color of the water. The rest of us need the farmers. This is what a river teaches, if
you live beside it long enough: that repetition is how a place says a thing
carefully.

# waxseal

## Inputs

- API_TOKEN env var
- in/*.png batch
- --threshold float flag

waxseal began as a weekend whim and outgrew the weekend. The name comes from the
sealing wax on my grandfather's letters, which he pressed with a thumb instead of a
stamp because, he said, a thumb can't be borrowed.

The tool stamps PNGs with an invisible seal: a few low bits per channel, imperceptible
on any screen, durable through most resizes. It was written for a newspaper archive
that kept losing track of which crops had been approved.

There is no grand design document. The whole thing fits on two screens, reads like a
letter, and has survived three archive migrations by being too small to break.

# ledgerctl

## Outputs

- out/report.csv
- exit code 0 or 3
- stderr run summary

ledgerctl got its name from the shoebox of receipts my aunt kept for a corner shop
she ran for thirty years. The shoebox was the ledger. It was perfect. Nobody ever
disputed an entry twice.

The tool checks a directory of expense scans against a supplier list and writes up
what it finds. It was built for one accountant who asked for "something that doesn't
have a manual." It doesn't. The help text is four lines and a joke.

The development notes are just dated sentences in a text file, which the accountant
has read and I have not. She says the tool "behaves," which is the only review any
software has ever earned, and the only one I trust.

# bricklane

## Assumptions

- assumes systemd 254+
- assumes /var/cache writable
- assumes UTC clock sync

bricklane takes a directory of loose web assets and flattens it into a single
hash-named bundle, the way a bricklane flattens cobblestones into something a cart
can trust. The name was my wife's. She wins.

It exists because a client's site had 4,000 assets and a deployment script with 4,000
opinions. One Saturday of stubbornness later, there was one tool and no opinions.

The code is deliberately dull: no plugins, no config grammar, no ambitions. It does
one pass, prints what it did, and gets out of the way. Dull software ages well. This
one has aged three years and counting, which in web-tool time is a dynasty.

# tidegauge-lite

## Calibration

- p=0.31 vs null 0.52
- MAE 0.04 vs 0.09 baseline
- offset -0.7 mm nominal

tidegauge-lite is a pressure sensor, a soda bottle, and about two hundred lines of
firmware, bolted to a pier that my uncle has fished from since 1974. The bottle is
the stilling well. The pier is the tripod. The uncle is the maintenance contract.

The harbor council wanted a gauge; the quotes came back at the price of a car. So we
built the cheap one and spent a full autumn on the tuning, walking the pier at low
water with a tape measure and a thermos, adjusting until the readings agreed with
the old float gauge on the far wall.

It has run through two winters now. The firmware is stable, the bottle is
replaceable for pocket change, and my uncle reports the fish don't mind it, which
was never a requirement but is noted here anyway.

# fernmill

A small log shipper for small machines. fernmill watches a log directory, cuts the
stream into compressed chunks, and hands them onward. It was written for a fleet of
warehouse scanners that could not run anything heavier, and it has never grown up,
on purpose.

## Audience

- On-call operators consume fernmill's alert stream during incidents, arriving from the paging runbook.
- New developers reach the codebase via the repo's CONTRIBUTING guide after the monthly onboarding email.

## Outputs

- Writes rotated, gzip log chunks to `out/chunks/`.
- Emits a one-page nightly summary to stderr when run with `--summary`.

## Composition

- Consumes syslog forwarded by relayd over a local Unix socket.
- Publishes finished chunks to the warehouse importer's staging queue.

## Calibration

- 99.2% chunk fidelity against the reference replayer across a 30-day replay.
- 3x faster throughput than the legacy shipper it replaced, measured on the same fleet.

The code stays boring by decree. The README is one screen. The whole project fits in
an afternoon's read, and the maintainers intend to keep it that way for as long as
the scanners keep scanning.

# slatecarve

slatecarve is a data migration tool for one very old media archive: it reads a
manifest, plans the move from the legacy store, and carves records into the new
schema. It runs rarely and must be right every time, which shaped everything about
it.

## Inputs

- Reads `manifest.toml` at the repository root for record mappings.
- Requires a read-only dump of the legacy store mounted at `/mnt/legacy`.

## Mode

- One-shot per release; reruns are no-ops on rows already migrated.
- Supports `--dry-run`, which plans the full move and writes nothing.

## Failure Modes

- Aborts on schema drift between the dump and the manifest, leaving a resume marker at the last clean record.
- Retries store lock timeouts three times, then halts and writes a partial-ledger note for the operator.

## Lifecycle

- v2 deprecates the flat manifest format; removal is planned for v3.
- Changes are recorded in `CHANGELOG.md` under Keep-a-Changelog headings.

The tool has migrated four collections so far, each with a dress rehearsal against a
copied dump first. The archive staff call it "the chisel," and have asked, twice,
that nothing about it ever change.
